objectives: Describe the paradox of knowledge and say why more facts can mean less understanding.
Tell knowing and understanding apart, and name the distinction that separates them.
Name the parts of an understanding: the recall, the evidence, the connections, the patterns and the explanation.
Compare knowing and understanding on six points, using a table of your own.
Turn one fact into understanding with six steps that work at the bench, in a meeting and in a study group.
Ask the questions that turn an answer into understanding: what it assumes, what would make it false, what it touches.
Explain why more information does not help when the facts are not joined to anything.

sections.body:
The paradox of knowledge is easy to state and hard to live with. A person collects more facts and understands no more. The shelf of manuals grows. The answers on the screen arrive faster. The understanding of the job stays where it was.

Five words carry the whole subject, and each one needs a sentence of its own. A **fact** is a piece of information that can be checked: it is true, or it is not. **Understanding** is a set of relations: it says why a fact holds, when it stops holding, and what would change it. **Structure** is the arrangement of those relations, so that a new fact has somewhere to go. **Recall** is the ability to bring a fact back into the mind when it is needed. **Knowledge** is what a person has when they can recall facts, use them to answer a question, and say why they hold.

The whole difference sits in one **distinction**: having the answer is not the same as knowing where the answer came from and when it holds. A sheet of formulas hands over the answer. It never says which case the formula was written for, and it never says what you do when the case is different. The reader who holds the sheet and the reader who can work the case are in two different places, and both of them can look very well informed. There is no figure here that you can check on a page, so this article names the difference and gives you the words for it instead of a number.
examples: I have the answer, but I do not know when it applies.
The facts are on the sheet; the understanding is in the head.
The manual gives the formula. It does not give the case it was written for.
sections.heading: The paradox: more facts, no more understanding

terms.example: He had the facts and the knowledge, because he could say why the pump behaved that way.
terms.gloss: What a person has when they can recall facts, use them to answer a question, and say why they hold.

terms.example: The distinction between the answer and the reason matters in every report.
terms.gloss: The act of saying what makes two things different, so that the reader does not confuse them.

sections.body:
Knowing, in the narrow sense, means the facts are there when you need them. You can recall them without looking. You can find them again in a manual, on a ticket, in a message from a colleague. A fact that was read once and is never found again is a fact that was lost.

Facts are cheap. You can copy one, store it, repeat it, print it on a sheet. Copying costs nothing and adds nothing: the copy does not know where the original came from. A list of two hundred definitions is two hundred lines to search through, not two hundred things you know. The knowledge is in what you can do at the moment the search fails. A fact that supports a claim, that the pump will not overheat at this load, is **evidence**; evidence is what a claim rests on, and it is worth more than the fact it came from.

Take the plain case: a worker reads a book of formulas on a plane. On landing, the book is in the bag and the formulas are in the head. Two weeks later the same worker has to size a pump that is not in the book. The formulas that were read are of no use, because the case in front of him is not a case in the book. The one formula he can derive from the pump's own data is the one that works. The book gave him facts and evidence. The pump asks him for understanding.

Knowing is necessary. It is not enough. You need the facts first, and then you need the relations between them.
examples: The formula is in the book; the knowledge is in the head.
I can recall the number, but I cannot use it on this case.
The log is evidence; the opinion is not.
sections.heading: What knowing is: facts you can find again

terms.example: My recall of the formula is good; my recall of the reason behind it is not.
terms.gloss: The ability to bring a fact back into the mind when it is needed, without looking it up.

terms.example: The temperature log is evidence that the pump ran hot.
terms.gloss: A fact that supports a claim, so that the claim does not rest on opinion alone.

sections.body:
Understanding is an arrangement. Every fact is joined to other facts, and the join carries what the fact alone does not hold: why it is true, when it stops being true, what would change it, and which other facts it touches. The join between two facts is a **connection**, and a connection is what lets a new fact be placed instead of merely stored. A shelf of facts with no connections between them answers no question, however full the shelf is.

Take the same example again. The reader who can derive the formula from the pump's data is in a different place from the reader who can only find the page. The first reader can answer a question the book never asked. The second can only answer the questions the book listed. When several facts take the same shape, and the same relation keeps coming back, that shape is a **pattern**. A pattern is found faster than the facts that make it, and it is what lets one case tell you what to watch for in the next one.

An **explanation** says why a fact holds, in words somebody else can follow. It says more than the result. The result says what happened; the explanation says why it happened and when it would not happen. Without one, the reader has to accept the fact on the authority of the page, and a page cannot be asked whether it is right.

Understanding is not a feeling and it is not a mood of confidence. It is a test you can pass or fail: say why the fact holds, say when it stops holding, say what would change it, and say which other facts it touches. A person who can do that has understanding, whatever they have read.
examples: I can find the page, but I cannot derive the formula.
The connection between the load and the valve is what the manual left out.
His explanation of the fault was better than the manual, because it said why.
sections.heading: What understanding is: a set of relations

terms.example: There is a connection between the load on the pump and the life of the seal.
terms.gloss: A link between two facts, so that one explains, limits or changes the other.

terms.example: The same pattern is in all three faults: the seal starts to leak before the part fails.
terms.gloss: A shape that several facts share, which is easier to see than the facts themselves.

terms.example: The explanation of the fault was better than the manual, because it said why the seal failed.
terms.gloss: An account that says why a fact holds, in words somebody else can follow.

sections.body:
Each row asks one question and answers it twice: once from the side of knowing, once from the side of understanding. The test used on each row is the **criterion**: for knowing it is whether the answer is right, for understanding it is whether you can say why the answer holds and where it stops holding.

Two rows matter most at work. The fourth: a list of answers goes out of date quietly, because nothing in it says when it was true, so you find out from the customer. A set of relations goes out of date loudly, because a change in one fact travels to the facts it was joined to. The sixth: a list is usually lost with the place that held it, the old laptop, the closed ticket, the manual in a cabinet, while a set of relations is lost in small pieces, one forgotten join at a time. That loss is the quiet one, because every piece is still there.
examples: Knowing gives the answer; understanding gives the reason and the limit.
The list is out of date, and nothing in it says so.
A change in one fact shows up in the facts it was joined to.
sections.heading: Knowing and understanding, side by side

rows: It is the facts you hold and can recall.
It is the arrangement of those facts and the reasons behind them.
You ask whether the answer is right.
You ask why it holds, when it stops holding, and what would change it.
You add one more answer to the list.
You join a new fact to what you already hold, and something moves.
What it does when the facts change
It goes out of date quietly, and nothing in it says when it was true.
The change shows up early, because the fact was joined to other facts.
By a list, a manual, a sheet of formulas, a file of notes.
By what you can say: the reason, the limit, the case it came from.
It is lost with the place that held it: the old laptop, the closed ticket, the manual in a cabinet.
It is lost slowly, one connection at a time, and nobody notices.

terms.example: The criterion for a useful fault report is not the length of it but the reason in it.
terms.gloss: The test that says whether something is good enough, or true enough.

sections.body:
Six steps turn one fact into something you can use. They take about ten minutes, they work at the bench, in a meeting and in a study group, and they are not a study programme. They are one small routine, applied to one fact at a time.

The order matters. Writing the fact in your own words comes first, because the words of the author are not yet yours. The assumptions come next, because a fact that assumes something you have not checked is a fact you will use in the wrong place. What would make it false comes third, because that is the question that gives a fact edges. The joins to what you already hold come fourth. The real case comes fifth. The last step, teaching it to somebody else and watching where you cannot explain, is the honest test: the gap you find there is the gap you still have to close.

Steps written in an order another person can follow are a **method**. A method is worth writing down, because it is the one part of the work that does not depend on the person who did it. If a colleague can run it on a fact you have never seen, it is a method. If only you can, it is a habit.
examples: In your own words: if you cannot say it, you do not have it yet.
What would make this false?
The method works in a meeting as well as at the bench.
sections.heading: How to turn a fact into understanding
steps: Write the fact in your own words, without looking at the source, using the words you would use when you explain it to a colleague.
Ask what it assumes: what must already be true for the fact to hold, and do you know that?
Ask what would make it false: write down the case where the fact stops being true.
Join it to two facts you already have, and say in one sentence how the new fact changes the old ones.
Use it once on a real case: a job, a customer, a repair, a meeting, and write down what the fact decided.
Teach it to somebody else, and watch where you cannot explain. That is the gap you still have to close.

terms.example: The method is six steps, and any of us can run it on a new fact.
terms.gloss: A set of steps written in an order that another person can follow.

sections.body:
Keep a question in front of the reading. A fact that answers a question you care about stays with you; a fact with no question behind it becomes a line in a list. Read the manual for the question you went there with.

Write the reason, not only the result. A **rule** says what to do in a case; an **exception** is the case where the rule does not hold, and the rule is not wrong. The rule tells the colleague what to do; the exception tells the colleague when to stop, and it is the part that stops the rule from being wrong in the wrong place. Use one new idea in a real case the same week. A fact used on a live job in the same week becomes part of the work; a fact read and shelved stays a fact. Ask what the author would say if the case were different. The answer is usually a **case** the author had in mind: a size, a material, a customer, a temperature. Ask which one, and the rule becomes usable instead of merely correct.

None of this is a study method. These are four small habits, and each one keeps a fact close to the reason it holds.
examples: The rule is right, and the case is different.
Write the reason, not only the result.
Which case was the author thinking of?
sections.heading: Four habits that keep facts and understanding together

terms.example: The rule says to tighten the bolt to a stated torque, and it says nothing about the old bolt.
terms.gloss: A statement of what to do in a case, written for the situation the author had in mind.

terms.example: The exception is written under the rule: never on a seized bolt.
terms.gloss: The case in which a rule does not hold, and the rule is not wrong.

terms.example: This case is not the case the manual was written for.
terms.gloss: The situation in front of you, with its own conditions, not the generic one.

sections.body:
These are the sentences that turn a fact into work. They are short on purpose: a question of four words stops a meeting, and a paragraph of explanation does not.

Use the first two when somebody offers a fact without a reason. Use the rest when you want the reason yourself, or when you want to hand the fact to somebody else.
examples: Here is the fact. What does it assume?
What is the reason behind that conclusion?
Which case was that written for?
What would make this false?
The manual gives the answer; I want the reason.
I can recall the number, but I cannot use it here.
That is a fact, not an explanation.
sections.heading: Sentences you can use

sections.body:
Three ordinary situations make the paradox worse.

The first is speed. Facts arrive faster than they can be joined: a new document every hour, every one of them correct, none of them joined to anything. A large pile of true statements with no relations between them cannot answer a question. The **relevance** of a fact is the way it bears on the question being asked, and it is what turns material into something a person can use. A page that bears on nothing is not knowledge and it is not useless either: it is weight.

The second is the lookup. The answer is found instead of understood: the page is found, the number is copied, the case in front of you is not the case in the book, and the answer is wrong. The lookup is faster than the thinking, and the thinking is what would have caught it. The third is the rule without its case: the person knows the rule and not the situation the rule was written for, so the rule is applied where it does not hold, and nobody says so, because the rule itself says nothing about where it stops. The **context** is what tells you which situation you are in, and it is the thing a fact on its own cannot carry.

So the answer to information is not more information. It is structure: the joins that let a fact answer a question nobody asked when you learned it. A library with no index is the same as no library, because the books may all be there and the reader still cannot find the one that answers the question. That is the paradox in one sentence, and it is worth keeping in mind before you read one more manual.
examples: More documents will not help; the answer is the joins.
The rule was written for a different case.
A library with no index is the same as no library.
sections.heading: Where more knowledge still makes things worse

terms.example: In the context of a night shift, that warning means something different.
terms.gloss: The situation around a fact that decides what the fact means.

terms.example: The relevance of the log is clear once you know which question you are asking.
terms.gloss: The way a fact bears on the question being asked.

item.summary: Knowing more facts does not make a person understand more. After reading this you can tell knowing from understanding, name the words that carry the difference, compare the two on six points, turn one fact into understanding with six steps, and ask the questions that make an answer usable at work.
item.title: The Paradox of Knowledge: Why Knowing More Is Not Understanding More
